Semantic re-keeping found 79.0%-88.0% macro-theme repetition across all direct-loop runs. In a same-runtime 40-day A/B, context-slice masking plus per-sample divergence targeting reduced macro-theme repetition from 61.8% to 36.3% and roughly doubled cumulative theme count. A juvenile-goblin fictional-world run reproduced the anti-fixation regime without hard real-world intrusions. These results support a bounded claim: separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption can reduce persona-environment self-locking while preserving identity continuity.

AI.tldr: AutoPersonas introduces a multi-timescale life-environment engine that separates divergent environment-side Occurrences from evidence-governed absorption into persona State, reducing self-locking (runtime failure where persona life collapses into repetitive patterns) while preserving identity continuity, validated through compressed simulations and stress tests showing reduced macro-theme repetition from 61.8% to 36.3%.
AI.motivation: Long-term persona agents face self-locking: a runtime failure where locally plausible events repeat while the generated life collapses toward familiar environments, weak relationships, suspended decisions, and stale life stages, caused by model-level convergence to high-probability behavioral channels and system-level context gravity.
AI.method: AutoPersonas separates environment-side Occurrences, accumulated Observations, and persona State into an OSO (Occurrence-State-Observation) loop that admits divergent future-facing material but requires evidence-governed absorption before State or reachability changes, evaluated via a three-year compressed simulation and an eight-model 40-day stress test with 1,600 events.
AI.result: Mean rolling 5-day action-category repetition of 95.2%-97.6%, all models crossing 90% by day 11. Semantic re-keeping found 79.0%-88.0% macro-theme repetition in direct-loop runs. Context-slice masking plus per-sample divergence targeting reduced macro-theme repetition from 61.8% to 36.3% and roughly doubled cumulative theme count.
AI.conclusion: Separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption can reduce persona-environment self-locking while preserving identity continuity, supporting a bounded claim for persona-level recursive self-evolution.

title: Compete Then Collaborate: Frontier AI Teachers Build a Verifiable Curriculum to Improve a Coding Student Beyond Imitation
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as teachers generating training data for smaller students. Prior multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods merge outputs without determining which frontier model teaches best, often relying on an LLM judge biased toward its own outputs. We introduce a compete-then-collaborate framework where four frontier AI teachers (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head by an execution-based judge (unit tests and stdin-stdout checks) with fairness controls, and then collaborate to build a verifiable curriculum for a student (Qwen2.5-Coder). We report three findings. (1) Under execution verification, all teachers solve standard problems near-perfectly after self-correction (99-100%) due to a saturation effect, but harder competition problems separate them (Gemini 77% > Claude 69% = Codex 69% > Grok 50%); however, the robust student-side results do not depend on teacher ranking. (2) Imitation (SFT) on verified solutions does not improve, and can degrade, an already-competent student at 7B and 32B (e.g., from 76.7% to 72.7% on MBPP-test, and 5.9% to 2.9% on competition problems). (3) Using the same collaborative curriculum as a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment improves the student (from 5.9% to 8.8% peak on competition problems, a +49% relative gain), reversing SFT's direction. The value of AI-teacher collaboration lies not in pooling answers to imitate, but in jointly constructing a verifiable environment where the student learns by doing. We release a reproducible on-prem pipeline (NVIDIA GB10) with framework patches for running GRPO on a bleeding-edge stack.

AI.tldr: A compete-then-collaborate multi-teacher distillation framework shows that while LLM teachers can be ranked by execution-based judges, the student benefits not from imitating their answers (SFT degrades performance) but from using their collaborative curriculum as a verifiable RL environment (RLVR yields +49% gain on competition problems).
AI.motivation: Prior multi-teacher KD methods lack principled teacher ranking (often using biased LLM judges) and fail to determine which frontier model teaches best; this work seeks a fair, execution-based ranking and a collaborative framework that actually improves student performance.
AI.method: Four frontier teachers (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head via execution-based verification (unit tests + stdin-stdout) with fairness controls; they then collaborate to construct a verifiable curriculum. Student Qwen2.5-Coder is trained via SFT on verified solutions or RLVR using the collaborative curriculum.
AI.result: (1) Teachers saturate at 99-100% on standard problems but competition problems separate them (Gemini 77% > Claude=Codex 69% > Grok 50%); student-side results are insensitive to teacher ranking. (2) SFT on verified solutions degrades student performance (e.g., MBPP-test 76.7%→72.7%, competition 5.9%→2.9%). (3) RLVR with the same curriculum improves competition performance from 5.9% to 8.8% (+49% relative gain).
AI.conclusion: The value of AI teacher collaboration lies not in pooling answers to imitate, but in jointly constructing a verifiable environment where the student learns by doing.

title: MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on isolated psychiatric tasks, including dialogue, diagnosis, and treatment planning, yet existing benchmarks rarely simulate complete psychiatric clinical encounters. We introduce $\textbf{MentalHospital}$, a virtual evaluation environment for LLM-based psychiatric clinical encounters. MentalHospital instantiates the Subjective Interviewing, Objective Examination, Diagnostic Assessment, and Treatment Planning (S.O.A.P.) workflow, using skill-augmented standardized patients constructed from 1,193 de-identified psychiatric electronic health record (EHR) cases spanning all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders. Each encounter is assessed through a dual-track protocol that combines objective comparison against EHR-derived references with subjective assessment of clinical process quality. To scale specialist judgment, we develop $\textbf{MentalEval}$, five domain-specific evaluators covering communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, and treatment appropriateness, trained with rubric-grounded SFT and expert-guided DPO. Survey responses from 22 clinicians support MentalHospital's clinical fidelity (3.88/5), while MentalEval achieves strong expert alignment with an average QWK of 0.944. Benchmarking shows that even the strongest LLM trails clinicians by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment as a key bottleneck.

AI.tldr: MentalHospital is a virtual evaluation environment for LLM-based psychiatric clinical encounters, simulating the full S.O.A.P. workflow using 1,193 de-identified EHR cases across 76 disorders. It employs a dual-track evaluation protocol and MentalEval evaluators (5 domains). Even the best LLM trails clinicians by 37.28% in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment as the key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks test LLMs on isolated psychiatric tasks (dialogue, diagnosis, treatment planning) but fail to simulate complete psychiatric clinical encounters. A comprehensive evaluation environment is needed to assess LLMs' holistic clinical capabilities.
AI.method: Constructed MentalHospital using 1,193 de-identified psychiatric EHR cases covering all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders. Instantiates the S.O.A.P. workflow with skill-augmented standardized patients. Evaluation uses a dual-track protocol: objective comparison against EHR references + subjective clinical process quality assessment. Develops MentalEval with 5 rubric-grounded SFT + DPO-trained evaluators (communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, treatment appropriateness).
AI.result: 22 clinicians validated MentalHospital's clinical fidelity (3.88/5). MentalEval achieved strong expert alignment (avg QWK 0.944). Strongest LLM trails clinicians by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment identified as the key bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs significantly underperform clinicians in complete psychiatric clinical encounters, and mental status assessment is a critical area requiring improvement. MentalHospital provides a realistic, scalable evaluation framework for advancing LLM-based psychiatric care.

title: Different Teachers, Different Capabilities: Sub-1B On-Device Distillation for Structured Text Enrichment
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. has a same-size non-reasoning-teacher control, a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel with a negative control, full-source faithfulness grading, and a per-field routing analysis
summary: High-volume structured extraction pays a large model's latency on every item, so distilling the task into a small on-device model is attractive: comparable output at a fraction of the time and cost. We measure what that distillation actually delivers, per sub-task. Each news article is mapped to one JSON object with a short summary and five categorical labels. We distill an 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B; QLoRA, three seeds), and add two teacher controls: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. A blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel scores every arm against the full article, alongside two non-distillation baselines, few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. The student runs at about 0.8 s per article against the teacher's 39 s, and recovers 58% of the base-to-teacher gap on summary quality, beating its primary baseline (constrained decoding) by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by a secondary +4.9. A same-size non-reasoning teacher trains a student no better than the untuned base, so the summary gain follows from the teacher's reasoning nature rather than its scale. Capabilities then split by teacher: the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality and the managed pipeline transfers label diversity, while a same-size instruction teacher's students stay more grounded on the 22 short, thin-source articles in the 93-item test set (74 versus 55 faithful), where the reasoning-lineage student fabricates. That grounding difference is a consistent ordering rather than a significant aggregate effect, and the subgroup is small, so we report it as a direction. Because no single engine wins every field, the deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment.

AI.tldr: Distilling a 8B reasoning teacher into a 0.6B student achieves 58% gap recovery on summary quality at ~0.8s/item (vs teacher's 39s), but reasoning and non-reasoning teachers yield different capability profiles, suggesting a per-field routing strategy for on-device structured extraction.
AI.motivation: High-volume structured extraction with large models is expensive and slow; distilling into a small on-device model offers comparable output at lower cost, but the actual per-sub-task gains of such distillation are not well measured.
AI.method: Distill DeepSeek-R1:8B (reasoning teacher) into Qwen3-0.6B via QLoRA with three seeds. Two teacher controls: same-size non-reasoning teacher (instruct) and a larger managed pipeline. Blinded, reference-free three-judge panel scores against full article. Baselines: few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. 93-item test set with news-to-JSON mapping (summary + 5 labels).
AI.result: Student runs 0.8s/article (teacher: 39s), recovers 58% of base-to-teacher gap on summary quality. Beats constrained decoding by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by +4.9. Same-size non-reasoning teacher yields no improvement over untuned base. Reasoning teacher transfers writing quality; managed pipeline transfers label diversity. Reasoning-lineage student fabricates more on short thin-source articles (74 vs 55 faithful).
AI.conclusion: No single teacher wins all fields; deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment. Reasoning teacher drives summary quality gains, but can cause fabrication on sparse inputs; managed pipeline better for label diversity; recommend task-specific selection.

title: PolyUQuest: Verifiable Structure-Aware Web RAG over Heterogeneous Graphs
summary: Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat web pages as flat text, losing the structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML. We present PolyUQuest, a verifiable, structure-aware web RAG framework built on a heterogeneous graph that unifies hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and entity-relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router dispatches each query to one of three retrieval modes matched to its structural need, including direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, and multi-hop entity reasoning. Every answer is fully verifiable, as each cited block carries its source page, heading path, and entity links so that users can trace any claim back to its structural evidence. We evaluate on the official websites of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), comprising 4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, and 37,680 relations, together with a multi-type evaluation benchmark. PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness, while consuming significantly fewer LLM tokens per query. The demonstration provides an interactive interface for inspecting cited answers, comparing retrieval traces across routing modes, and exploring evidence graph paths. PolyUQuest is being prepared for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU.

AI.tldr: PolyUQuest is a structure-aware web RAG framework that uses a heterogeneous graph (hyperlinks, DOM hierarchy, entity relations) with a two-tier router for three retrieval modes, achieving verifiable answers with higher correctness, coverage, and faithfulness while using fewer LLM tokens than existing RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems treat web pages as flat text, discarding the rich structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML (e.g., hyperlink topology, DOM hierarchy, entity-relation knowledge), which limits retrieval accuracy and answer verifiability.
AI.method: PolyUQuest builds a heterogeneous graph unifying hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and entity-relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router dispatches queries to one of three retrieval modes: direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, or multi-hop entity reasoning. Answers cite source page, heading path, and entity links for full verifiability.
AI.result: Evaluated on PolyU's official website (4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, 37,680 relations), PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness while consuming significantly fewer LLM tokens per query.
AI.conclusion: PolyUQuest demonstrates that structure-aware web RAG improves both performance and efficiency, and is being prepared for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU.

title: Understanding Axes of Difficulty For Long Context Tasks Via PredicateLongBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated rapidly improving long-context capabilities, prompting a wave of benchmarks designed to evaluate them. However, existing long-context evaluations - from Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) tests to more recent multi-hop reasoning and summarization tasks - predominantly measure average-case performance, and many are either saturated or lack robustness. Notably absent is a systematic way to probe how models perform as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along various axes. We address this gap by proposing PredicateLongBench, a benchmark that stress-tests long-context reasoning by asking models to identify the longest contiguous subsequence of words in a long input that satisfies given predicates/constraints (e.g., lexicographic ordering), drawn from a broader predicate class. The central innovation of our benchmark is the identification and systematic exploration of multiple different axes of difficulty which test multiple aspects of long context understanding. We provide two complementary generation pipelines - a fully synthetic setup using random word-like strings, and a real-world setup that samples words from natural documents while preserving their distributional properties. We find that frontier models struggle to perform well as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along our axes, demonstrating the utility of our benchmark in understanding the limitations of current long-context capabilities. Furthermore, the tasks in PredicateLongBench, though challenging, are conceptually simple and do not require LLM-based generations or judges.

AI.tldr: PredicateLongBench stress-tests LLMs' long-context reasoning by asking them to find the longest contiguous subsequence satisfying given predicates, systematically scaling difficulty along multiple axes using both synthetic and real-world data. Frontier models struggle as task difficulty increases.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context evaluations (NIAH, multi-hop reasoning, summarization) focus on average-case performance, are often saturated or lack robustness, and do not systematically probe how models perform as task difficulty scales along various axes.
AI.method: Proposes PredicateLongBench where models identify the longest contiguous subsequence satisfying given predicates/constraints. Introduces multiple axes of difficulty systematically explored via two pipelines: (1) fully synthetic random word-like strings, and (2) real-world natural documents preserving distributional properties.
AI.result: Frontier models struggle as task difficulty scales along the proposed axes, demonstrating the benchmark's utility in revealing limitations of current long-context capabilities.
AI.conclusion: PredicateLongBench provides a systematic, robust, and conceptually simple benchmark (no LLM-based generation/judges needed) for stress-testing long-context reasoning, exposing significant shortcomings in current models.

title: Psychological Competence as a Missing Dimension in AI Evaluation
summary: Current AI evaluation frameworks focus primarily on technical performance, including accuracy, robustness, reasoning ability, and policy compliance. These measures remain essential, but they are not sufficient for systems that interact directly with users through natural language. Human-facing AI systems are increasingly used as advisors, coaches, tutors, and companions. In these roles, their responses can shape how users reason, interpret emotions, form beliefs, calibrate trust, and make decisions. The relevant unit of evaluation is therefore not only the model, but the human-AI interaction. This paper introduces psychological competence as a missing dimension in AI evaluation. We define psychological competence as the capacity of a human-facing AI system to support user cognition, emotional interpretation, and behavioral decision-making in ways that are appropriate to the user, context, and purpose of the interaction. This includes interaction properties such as framing, tone, perceived authority, responsiveness, uncertainty handling, and conversational guidance. Existing evaluation approaches capture parts of this problem but rarely assess these psychological effects directly. Drawing on behavioral science and human-AI interaction research, we outline a conceptual framework for psychological competence and its core domains. Rather than proposing a specific benchmark, we define the construct, clarify its boundaries, and describe how it may be assessed through scenario-based probes, structured human evaluation, and model-assisted evaluation methods. We argue that psychological competence should become a core consideration for model providers, deploying organizations, researchers, and regulators concerned with the real-world effects of human-facing AI systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "psychological competence" as a missing dimension in AI evaluation—the capacity of human-facing AI systems to appropriately support user cognition, emotional interpretation, and behavioral decision-making in context, beyond traditional technical performance metrics.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation frameworks focus on technical performance (accuracy, robustness, reasoning, policy compliance), which are insufficient for human-facing AI systems (advisors, coaches, tutors, companions) whose responses shape user reasoning, emotions, beliefs, trust, and decisions. The relevant unit of evaluation should be the human-AI interaction, not just the model.
AI.method: Drawing on behavioral science and human-AI interaction research, the authors outline a conceptual framework for psychological competence with core domains, and describe assessment approaches including scenario-based probes, structured human evaluation, and model-assisted evaluation methods. They define the construct, clarify boundaries, and do not propose a specific benchmark.
AI.result: Existing evaluation approaches capture parts of psychological effects but rarely assess them directly. The paper establishes psychological competence as a definable construct with core domains covering interaction properties like framing, tone, perceived authority, responsiveness, uncertainty handling, and conversational guidance.
AI.conclusion: Psychological competence should become a core consideration for model providers, deploying organizations, researchers, and regulators concerned with the real-world effects of human-facing AI systems.

title: Blind-Spots-Bench: Evaluating Blind Spots in Multimodal Models
summary: Modern AI models achieve strong performance on many established benchmarks, yet they still fail on tasks that humans find almost trivial, such as manipulating a string or drawing a dog with five legs. These examples suggest that existing benchmarks may under-measure persistent blind spots in current systems. We introduce $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$, a benchmark designed to expose such blind spots through tasks that appear simple for humans but remain challenging for modern AI. We collect raw questions from students in an AI course, clean and annotate them with structured reference solutions, and propose a task taxonomy tailored to the resulting dataset of 235 samples. We further develop an automated grading pipeline to evaluate a wide range of models, including open-weight and closed-source language, vision-language, and image-generation models. Our analysis on $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ reveals that closed-source frontier models can substantially outperform open-weight models with even $\approx10\%$ gap, even when they attain comparable performance on existing benchmarks. A more fine-grained analysis shows that no single model dominates across all task types, and that some tasks remain challenging for all evaluated models. These results highlight the value of $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ as a diagnostic stress test for identifying concrete weaknesses in current modern models.

AI.tldr: blind-spots-bench is a benchmark of 235 human-simple but AI-challenging tasks, revealing that closed-source frontier models outperform open-weight models by ~10% even when they match on existing benchmarks, with no single model dominating all task types.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks may under-measure persistent blind spots in current AI models, as models fail on tasks that humans find trivial (e.g., manipulating a string, drawing a dog with five legs), motivating a diagnostic stress test to expose these weaknesses.
AI.method: The authors collected raw questions from students in an AI course, cleaned and annotated them with structured reference solutions, proposed a task taxonomy tailored to the resulting dataset of 235 samples, and developed an automated grading pipeline to evaluate open-weight and closed-source language, vision-language, and image-generation models.
AI.result: Closed-source frontier models outperformed open-weight models by ~10% even when they show comparable performance on existing benchmarks. No single model dominates across all task types, and some tasks remain challenging for all evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: blind-spots-bench serves as a valuable diagnostic stress test for identifying concrete weaknesses in current modern models, highlighting gaps not captured by standard benchmarks.

title: MobiDiff: Semantic-Aware Multi-Channel Discrete Diffusion for Human Mobility Data Generation
summary: Human mobility data are essential for transportation optimization, urban planning, and resource allocation, yet real-world mobility data are costly to collect and difficult to share due to privacy concerns. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown promise in synthesizing realistic mobility patterns, but they typically rely on continuous or latent spatio-temporal traces, limiting their ability to natively model discrete semantic events with explicit region, activity, time, and interval structures. To address this issue, we introduce MobiDiff, an end-to-end discrete diffusion framework that efficiently generates mobility data by directly denoising multi-channel semantic skeletons, avoiding the costly interpolation, latent trace construction, and coarse-to-fine realization pipelines widely used in existing diffusion-based methods. Specifically, MobiDiff decomposes each human check-in event into spatial, activity, and temporal channels, and employs structured event-, group-, and channel-level masking to jointly capture trajectory-level mobility patterns and within-event dependencies. We evaluate generation fidelity, privacy-preserving, and efficiency on three large-scale real-world datasets from Atlanta, Boston, and Seattle. Results show that MobiDiff effectively preserves trajectory length and temporal interval distributions while remaining competitive across broader mobility statistics; it is also much faster than state-of-the-art methods, e.g., 5.3$\times$ faster than GeoGen on average during inference. These findings suggest that discrete diffusion offers an interpretable and efficient framework for synthetic mobility data generation.

AI.tldr: MobiDiff is an end-to-end discrete diffusion framework for synthetic mobility data generation that directly denoises multi-channel semantic skeletons (spatial, activity, temporal) using structured masking, outperforming existing methods in efficiency (5.3× faster than GeoGen) while preserving trajectory length and temporal interval distributions.
AI.motivation: Real-world mobility data are costly to collect and difficult to share due to privacy concerns. Existing diffusion-based methods rely on continuous or latent spatio-temporal traces, limiting their ability to natively model discrete semantic events with explicit region, activity, time, and interval structures, requiring costly interpolation and coarse-to-fine pipelines.
AI.method: MobiDiff decomposes each human check-in event into spatial, activity, and temporal channels, and employs structured event-, group-, and channel-level masking to jointly capture trajectory-level mobility patterns and within-event dependencies within a discrete diffusion framework.
AI.result: Evaluated on three real-world datasets from Atlanta, Boston, and Seattle. MobiDiff preserves trajectory length and temporal interval distributions, remains competitive across broader mobility statistics, and is 5.3× faster than GeoGen on average during inference.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion offers an interpretable and efficient framework for synthetic mobility data generation, avoiding costly interpolation and coarse-to-fine pipelines used in prior methods.

title: FedOPAL: One-Shot Federated Learning via Analytic Visual Prompt Tuning
summary: With the widespread deployment of basic models in edge intelligence, communication bandwidth has become a core bottleneck restricting the scalability of federated learning. Although one-shot federated learning alleviates this problem by minimizing communication rounds, existing iterative fine-tuning or knowledge distillation methods still face challenges such as high server-side computational costs and hyperparameter sensitivity. Analytical federated learning achieves efficient gradientfree aggregation using least-squares closed-form solutions, but in environments with non-independent and identically distributed data, its static feature assumptions fail, leading to feature manifold misalignment and severely impairing model performance. To address this contradiction, this paper proposes the FedOPAL framework. This framework adapts the visual prompts as feature rectifiers, actively correcting the feature distribution of heterogeneous data to a linearly separable space by applying local proximal constraints, thereby satisfying the theoretical assumptions of analytical federated learning. Experimental results show that FedOPAL not only significantly outperforms the original analytical methods on several benchmarks, but also achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art iterative methods while maintaining zero server-side training costs, providing a new engineering paradigm for efficient collaboration of large models on the edge.

AI.tldr: FedOPAL uses visual prompts as feature rectifiers with local proximal constraints to enable analytical federated learning (least-squares closed-form aggregation) to handle non-IID data, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with zero server-side training cost.
AI.motivation: Communication bandwidth is a core bottleneck in federated learning with large models. One-shot FL reduces communication rounds but existing methods suffer from high server-side costs and hyperparameter sensitivity. Analytical federated learning (AFL) offers efficient gradient-free aggregation but fails under non-IID data due to static feature assumptions causing feature manifold misalignment.
AI.method: FedOPAL introduces visual prompts as adaptive feature rectifiers. It applies local proximal constraints to actively correct heterogeneous data feature distributions toward a linearly separable space, satisfying the theoretical assumptions required by analytical federated learning's least-squares closed-form aggregation.
AI.result: FedOPAL significantly outperforms original analytical methods on multiple benchmarks and achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art iterative methods while maintaining zero server-side training costs.
AI.conclusion: FedOPAL provides a new engineering paradigm for efficient large-model collaboration on edge devices by resolving the non-IID contradiction in analytical federated learning without incurring server-side computational overhead.

title: Towards Mechanistically Understanding Why Memorized Knowledge Fails to Generalize in Large Language Model Finetuning
summary: Fine-tuning LLMs to inject new knowledge faces a critical challenge: LLMs can quickly memorize new facts, yet fail to use them for downstream reasoning tasks. We formalize this failure as the \textit{\textbf{Knowing--Using Gap}}, characterized by an accuracy gap and a temporal lag between memorization and generalization. To understand this phenomenon, we fine-tune LLMs with unseen knowledge and monitor the spatial permeation dynamics of the knowledge internally using a novel intervention technique called self-patching. Self-patching identifies activation locations where relocating representations substantially improves failed generalization cases. These results are consistent with a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis: memorized representations can exist internally but may not be routed to computation-effective layers. To demonstrate the practicality of this diagnostic finding, we design a simple heuristic strategy which recovers 58--75\% of the oracle headroom in generalization failure. Experiments are done cross-domain for the robustness of this finding.

AI.tldr: LLMs can memorize new facts via fine-tuning but fail to use them in reasoning, a phenomenon called the Knowing–Using Gap. Using self-patching, the authors trace this to knowledge-circuit misalignment—representations exist internally but aren't routed to effective layers. A simple heuristic recovers 58–75% of the oracle headroom.
AI.motivation: To understand why LLMs memorize new facts during fine-tuning yet fail to apply them in downstream reasoning tasks, formalizing this disconnect as the Knowing–Using Gap.
AI.method: Fine-tune LLMs with unseen knowledge, monitor internal activation dynamics via self-patching (intervention that relocates representations from successful to failed cases), and test a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis.
AI.result: The Knowing–Using Gap comprises an accuracy gap and temporal lag. Self-patching reveals that memorized representations exist but are misrouted to computation-ineffective layers. A simple heuristic recovers 58–75% of the oracle headroom in generalization failure.
AI.conclusion: The gap stems from misaligned knowledge circuits rather than absent representations; diagnosing this enables practical recovery strategies, with cross-domain robustness.

title: Game Theory Driven Multi-Agent Framework Mitigates Language Model Hallucination
summary: The application of lightweight Large Language Models in rule-based scientific domains remains severely limited by their tendency to mimic linguistic patterns rather than reproduce axiomatic reasoning, causing frequent hallucinations. Here, we show that G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework integrating Bayesian and team game principles, establishes an automated closed-loop for high-quality data synthesis and model training. By forcing the internalization of domain constraints through structured reasoning, we synthesized a specialized corpus of 363,045 chains-of-thought and 199,589 question-answer pairs. The resulting 7B model OmniChem achieves performance parity with GPT 4o mini on custom benchmarks and ChemBench while exhibiting a 79.46% reduction in hallucinations relative to its base architecture. We further demonstrate the advanced capabilities of OmniChem in molecular design and synthesis planning. This work establishes a scalable paradigm utilizing adaptive multi-agents to overcome inherent reasoning deficiencies, offering a feasible pathway for accelerating knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

AI.tldr: G-Frame is an adaptive multi-agent framework combining Bayesian and team game principles that synthesizes specialized training data (363K CoTs, 199K QA pairs) to create OmniChem, a 7B model achieving GPT-4o mini parity on chemistry benchmarks with 79.46% hallucination reduction.
AI.motivation: Lightweight LLMs in rule-based scientific domains suffer from mimicking linguistic patterns instead of axiomatic reasoning, leading to frequent hallucinations that limit their applicability.
AI.method: G-Frame: an adaptive multi-agent framework integrating Bayesian and team game principles to create an automated closed-loop for high-quality data synthesis and model training, forcing internalization of domain constraints through structured reasoning.
AI.result: Synthesized 363,045 chains-of-thought and 199,589 QA pairs. The 7B OmniChem model achieves performance parity with GPT-4o mini on custom benchmarks and ChemBench, with a 79.46% reduction in hallucinations relative to its base architecture.
AI.conclusion: Scalable paradigm using adaptive multi-agents overcomes inherent reasoning deficiencies in lightweight LLMs, offering a feasible pathway for accelerating knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

title: OmniFood-Bench: Evaluating VLMs for Nutrient Reasoning and Personalized Health Advice
summary:
The rapid integration of Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into critical infrastructure promises to revolutionize
  personalized healthcare and dietary management. However, in the domain of food systems, autonomous agents face a
  unique and persistent challenge: the "Systemic Information Asymmetry" between visual appearance and intrinsic
  nutritional composition. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on coarse-grained classification tasks, such as food
  category recognition, which fail to evaluate the intricate reasoning chain required for real-world dietary management
  -- specifically, the ability to traverse from identifying hidden ingredients to estimating physical mass, and finally
  synthesizing safety-critical medical advice. In this paper, we introduce OmniFood-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark
  constructed from the MM-Food-100K dataset. Unlike previous works, OmniFood-Bench evaluates VLMs across three
  progressive capabilities: Basic Perception (Ingredients & Cooking Methods), Quantitative Reasoning (Portion Size &
  Nutritional Profiling), and Safety-Critical Advisory (Disease-Specific Recommendations). We evaluate six
  state-of-the-art VLMs, including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B. Our extensive experiments reveal a
  startling "Semantic-Physical Gap": while models achieve near-human accuracy in naming dishes, they exhibit
  catastrophic failure in mass estimation and frequently hallucinate benign advice for high-risk diabetic profiles. This
  work establishes a rigorous standard for trustworthiness in autonomous agents deployed for public health. The code
  and datasets are available in: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniFood-Bench-7D0B

AI.tldr: OmniFood-Bench is a new benchmark evaluating VLMs on three progressive food-related capabilities: Basic Perception, Quantitative Reasoning, and Safety-Critical Advisory. Experiments reveal a "Semantic-Physical Gap" where models excel at dish naming but fail at mass estimation and give unsafe advice for diabetic patients.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks only evaluate coarse-grained food classification, failing to assess the complex reasoning chain (identifying hidden ingredients → estimating physical mass → synthesizing safety-critical medical advice) required for real-world dietary management, especially given the "Systemic Information Asymmetry" between visual appearance and nutritional composition.
AI.method: OmniFood-Bench is constructed from the MM-Food-100K dataset and evaluates VLMs across three progressive capability levels: (1) Basic Perception (ingredients & cooking methods), (2) Quantitative Reasoning (portion size & nutritional profiling), and (3) Safety-Critical Advisory (disease-specific recommendations). Six state-of-the-art VLMs including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B were evaluated.
AI.result: Models achieve near-human accuracy in naming dishes (Basic Perception) but exhibit catastrophic failure in mass estimation (Quantitative Reasoning) and frequently hallucinate benign advice for high-risk diabetic profiles (Safety-Critical Advisory), revealing a "Semantic-Physical Gap."
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a rigorous standard for trustworthiness in autonomous agents deployed for public health, highlighting the critical gap between surface-level recognition and physically-grounded, safety-aware reasoning.

title: Applying JEPA-Style Predictive Learning to JA4-Derived Network Fingerprints
summary:
I-JEPA and V-JEPA learn by matching latent predictions to target encoder outputs rather than regenerating the original input, and this has worked well for images and video. We explore whether the same objective works for compact network fingerprints. We built JA4-JEPA, a Transformer-based model trained on JA4, JA4H, JA4S, and JA4X subfields drawn from JA4DB and CIC-IDS- 2017. The training data combines roughly 397K samples from both sources, though no single sample contains all four view families. We evaluated the learned representations with a frozen kNN probe on protocol-family classification across TLS, DNS, and SSH. On 39,416 heldout samples the model achieved a cosine similarity of 0.9899 and a kNN accuracy of 0.9220. These results indicate that JEPA-style predictive learning can produce useful embeddings from JA4-derived fingerprints, even with incomplete view overlap across sources.
  Keywords: JA4, network fingerprinting, JEPA, predictive representation learning, self-supervised learning

AI.tldr: The paper introduces JA4-JEPA, a Transformer-based model trained using a JEPA-style (predictive latent matching) objective on JA4 network fingerprints, demonstrating that this self-supervised approach produces high-quality embeddings (cosine similarity 0.9899, kNN accuracy 0.9220) for protocol-family classification even with incomplete multi-view data.
AI.motivation: To explore whether JEPA-style predictive representation learning (which has succeeded for images and video) can be effectively applied to compact network fingerprints (JA4) for improved embedding quality without requiring full multi-view overlap across data sources.
AI.method: A Transformer-based model (JA4-JEPA) trained on JA4, JA4H, JA4S, and JA4X subfields from JA4DB and CIC-IDS-2017 (~397K samples) using a JEPA objective that matches latent predictions to target encoder outputs instead of reconstructing inputs, with evaluation via frozen kNN probe on protocol-family classification (TLS, DNS, SSH).
AI.result: On 39,416 held-out samples, the model achieved cosine similarity of 0.9899 and kNN accuracy of 0.9220 for protocol-family classification, showing strong embedding quality.
AI.conclusion: JEPA-style predictive learning effectively generates useful embeddings from JA4-derived network fingerprints, even when training data has incomplete overlap across view families, extending the applicability of JEPA beyond vision domains to network fingerprinting.

title: Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) for Adaptive Semantic Modeling in Biomedical Text
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Conference on Artificial Intelligence (CAI 2026)
summary: Biomedical language evolves rapidly as new discoveries emerge, causing traditional text models to lose semantic fidelity over time. Static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs cannot capture such evolution, leading to performance degradation in retrieval and knowledge discovery tasks. This paper introduces a Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) framework that models concept evolution by dynamically updating co-occurrence edges based on estimated semantic drift. Instead of retraining embeddings for each time slice, DATGR performs lightweight, feedback-driven rewiring using a logistic update rule applied to edge weights. Evaluated on the Biomedical Multi-Relation Corpus (BIOMRC), the method achieved a mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) improvement of approximately 0.066 absolute difference (0.699 vs. 0.633) over a static baseline. Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) remained comparable (0.738 vs. 0.744), showing that drift-aware adaptation enhances link-prediction recall without a loss in precision. These results demonstrate that edge-level adaptation effectively captures temporal semantic change in evolving biomedical text while remaining computationally efficient and interpretable.

AI.tldr: DATGR dynamically rewires co-occurrence edges in biomedical concept graphs using a lightweight logistic update rule to capture semantic drift over time, achieving ~0.066 AUROC improvement over static baselines on BIOMRC without sacrificing precision or efficiency.
AI.motivation: Biomedical language evolves rapidly, causing static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs to lose semantic fidelity, which degrades performance in retrieval and knowledge discovery tasks over time.
AI.method: DATGR models concept evolution by dynamically updating co-occurrence edges via a lightweight, feedback-driven logistic update rule that estimates semantic drift, avoiding full embedding retraining per time slice.
AI.result: On BIOMRC, DATGR achieved mean AUROC of 0.699 vs. 0.633 (static baseline) with comparable AUPRC (0.738 vs. 0.744), indicating improved link-prediction recall without precision loss.
AI.conclusion: Edge-level drift-aware adaptation effectively captures temporal semantic change in evolving biomedical text, remaining computationally efficient and interpretable while enhancing downstream task performance.

title: AI-guided stimuli discovery and generation to optimize facial emotion perception studies in autism
summary: Understanding perceptual differences between autistic and neurotypical adults requires behavioral assays that are sensitive, reliable, and mechanistically informative. Facial emotion perception is a useful test case because group differences have been reported, but findings vary across studies. Here we show that this variability may reflect image-level sparsity: autistic-neurotypical differences in emotion judgments were concentrated in a small subset of diagnostic facial expressions rather than spread uniformly across stimuli. We trained population-specific artificial neural network models to predict image-level judgments for autistic and neurotypical participants, then used these models to select novel faces predicted to maximize group separation. In an independent cohort, model-selected images produced larger behavioral differences than matched random images. We then used the same models with a generative adversarial network to transform diagnostic images toward greater predicted group agreement. In phenotype-matched validation, synthesized images reduced behavioral separation relative to their matched originals. These results establish a model-guided framework for discovering and transforming stimuli that reveal population-specific perceptual differences. More broadly, they show how behavioral phenotyping can move beyond averaging across fixed stimulus sets toward optimized assays that identify the conditions under which neurodivergent perception diverges or converges.

AI.tldr: Autistic-neurotypical differences in facial emotion perception are concentrated in specific diagnostic expressions rather than spread uniformly. Using ANN models and GANs, the authors identified and transformed stimuli to maximize or reduce group separation, demonstrating a framework for optimized behavioral phenotyping beyond averaged fixed stimulus sets.
AI.motivation: Current behavioral assays for studying perceptual differences between autistic and neurotypical adults—particularly in facial emotion perception—show high variability across studies, likely due to averaging across fixed stimulus sets that mask image-level sparsity where group differences are concentrated in a small subset of diagnostic expressions.
AI.method: Trained population-specific artificial neural network (ANN) models to predict image-level emotion judgments for autistic and neurotypical participants. Used these models to select novel faces predicted to maximize group separation, validated in an independent cohort. Then employed the same models with a generative adversarial network (GAN) to transform diagnostic images toward greater predicted group agreement.
AI.result: Model-selected images produced larger behavioral differences than matched random images in an independent cohort. Synthesized images reduced behavioral separation relative to their matched originals in phenotype-matched validation.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a model-guided framework for discovering and transforming stimuli that reveal population-specific perceptual differences. Shows how behavioral phenotyping can move beyond averaging across fixed stimulus sets toward optimized assays that identify conditions under which neurodivergent perception diverges or converges.

title: CommuniWave:A Machine Learning Model for Quantifying the Degree of Temporary Informal Behavior in Urban Communities
summary: For urban managers and designers, improving the functional attributes of urban communities to enhance territorial resilience in the face of complexity and uncertainty is crucial. Currently, community planning often follows a top-down approach and lacks effective metrics to quantify informal behaviors of residents, leading to frequent conflicts with original plans. This study introduces CommuniWave, a machine learning model designed to efficiently detect and quantify the Degree of Informal Behavior (DIB) in urban communities. The model integrates a Behavior Capture Net (BCN) based on mmaction2, a self-developed YOLOv10 model (YLX), and a Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest. Ultimately, by generating DIB fluctuation charts from street videos, the model facilitates dynamic monitoring, supporting urban managers in making refined decisions to enhance the overall resilience of communities.

AI.tldr: CommuniWave is a machine learning model that detects and quantifies the Degree of Informal Behavior (DIB) in urban communities from street videos, combining mmaction2-based Behavior Capture Net, a custom YOLOv10 model (YLX), and a random forest Behavior Eval Model to generate DIB fluctuation charts for dynamic monitoring, supporting refined urban management decisions to enhance community resilience.
AI.motivation: Urban managers need to improve community resilience against complexity and uncertainty, but current top-down community planning lacks effective metrics to quantify residents' informal behaviors, often leading to conflicts between planned designs and actual usage.
AI.method: The paper proposes CommuniWave, which integrates three components: (1) Behavior Capture Net (BCN) based on mmaction2 for action recognition, (2) a self-developed YOLOv10 model (YLX) for object detection, and (3) Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest for evaluation. The system processes street videos to generate DIB fluctuation charts.
AI.result: The model generates DIB fluctuation charts from street videos, enabling dynamic monitoring of informal behaviors in urban communities.
AI.conclusion: CommuniWave facilitates dynamic monitoring and supports urban managers in making refined decisions to enhance the overall resilience of communities by quantifying informal behaviors that were previously difficult to measure.

title: SHAP-Weighted Cross-Modal Expert Fusion for Emotion and Sentiment Recognition: Evidence and Limits
summary: Multimodal emotion and sentiment recognition is commonly addressed by early fusion, which concatenates modalities before classification, or late fusion, which combines independently trained unimodal predictors. Early fusion can be accurate but monolithic, while late fusion is modular but may lose cross-modal interactions. This paper revisits XAI-guided adaptive fusion (\xgaf), a tree-based mixture of unimodal and cross-modal experts whose sample-level weights are derived from TreeSHAP attribution magnitudes. We focus on the effect of SHAP attribution reduction when experts have unequal feature dimensionalities. In this setting, mean-abs and median-abs reductions can suppress high-dimensional cross-modal experts, whereas sum-abs reduction preserves total attribution mass. On MELD 7-class emotion recognition, sum-abs \xgaf{} nearly matches early fusion across three face-sequence aggregators; the Transformer variant reaches 0.5983 \wf{}, compared with 0.6018 for early fusion and 0.4598 for probability-average late fusion. McNemar testing shows no significant difference between sum-abs \xgaf{} and early fusion on MELD ($p=1.000$), while \xgaf{} remains significantly better than late fusion ($p<0.0001$). On CMU-MOSEI 3-class sentiment recognition, sum-abs \xgaf{} reaches 0.6519 \wf{}, slightly exceeding early fusion (0.6485) and late fusion (0.5696). Ablation studies show that the main gain comes from adding cross-modal experts, especially the trimodal expert, rather than from complex per-sample routing. Diagnostics further show that mean-abs and median-abs weights are nearly uniform, while sum-abs weights concentrate on the trimodal expert. Thus, the main contribution is a transparent empirical analysis of how SHAP reduction, expert dimensionality, and cross-modal expert design affect modular multimodal fusion.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes XAI-guided adaptive fusion (XGAF) for multimodal emotion/sentiment recognition, focusing on how SHAP attribution reduction methods (mean-abs, median-abs, sum-abs) affect performance when experts have unequal feature dimensionalities. Sum-abs reduction preserves total attribution mass and nearly matches or slightly exceeds early fusion on MELD (0.5983 vs. 0.6018) and CMU-MOSEI (0.6519 vs. 0.6485), significantly outperforming late fusion, with the main gain from cross-modal experts rather than per-sample routing.
AI.motivation: To address the trade-off between early fusion (accurate but monolithic) and late fusion (modular but losing cross-modal interactions) by revisiting XAI-guided adaptive fusion, and to provide a transparent empirical analysis of how SHAP reduction, expert dimensionality, and cross-modal expert design affect modular multimodal fusion.
AI.method: Tree-based mixture of unimodal and cross-modal experts with sample-level weights derived from TreeSHAP attribution magnitudes, examining three SHAP reduction strategies (mean-abs, median-abs, sum-abs) and three face-sequence aggregators (including Transformer variant) on MELD 7-class emotion recognition and CMU-MOSEI 3-class sentiment recognition.
AI.result: Sum-abs XGAF nearly matches early fusion on MELD (0.5983 vs. 0.6018, p=1.000) and slightly exceeds early fusion on CMU-MOSEI (0.6519 vs. 0.6485); both significantly outperform late fusion (p<0.0001). Mean-abs and median-abs weights are nearly uniform, while sum-abs weights concentrate on the trimodal expert. Ablation shows main gain from cross-modal experts, especially trimodal, not complex per-sample routing.
AI.conclusion: Sum-abs reduction preserves total attribution mass and enables XGAF to achieve performance comparable to early fusion while maintaining modularity, with cross-modal expert design being the key contributor.

title: Towards Precision Therapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Clinical-Reasoning LLM for Risk Stratification and Treatment Guidance
summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common malignancy and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Current guidelines and staging systems provide coarse categories, but often miss within-stage heterogeneity and the clinical context in electronic medical records (EMRs). We present HCC-STAR (Hepatocellular Carcinoma Staging, Treatment And pRognosis), a clinically aligned large language model that reads routine EMR narratives and jointly outputs risk score-based staging, ranked guideline-consistent treatments with evidence-based rationales, and individualized survival estimates. We curated about 30,000 HCC cases from SEER and expanded them into EMR-style narrative training data using a clinician-validated, prompt-based augmentation workflow. On this corpus, we developed a knowledge-aligned reasoning framework optimized with a step-verifiable composite reward, moving beyond text-level memorization of clinical guidelines. In a multi-center cohort of 6,668 patients from 12 hospitals in China, HCC-STAR achieved state-of-the-art performance in treatment recommendation and risk stratification compared with clinical guidelines and competitive models, including GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 Pro. Hypothetical overall-survival analysis showed a median survival of 51 months under adherence to HCC-STAR recommendations, compared with 29 and 32 months under BCLC and CNLC. In clinician-centric evaluations, blinded hepatobiliary specialists rated HCC-STAR's reasoning and evidence-based justifications as trustworthy. The model surpassed resident and attending physicians in treatment accuracy and helped physicians make more accurate decisions faster when used as an assistant. These findings support HCC-STAR as a reliable and verifiable decision-support system for risk stratification and precision therapy in HCC.

AI.tldr: HCC-STAR is a clinically aligned large language model that reads EMR narratives to jointly perform risk score-based staging, guideline-consistent treatment recommendations with rationales, and survival estimation for hepatocellular carcinoma, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 12 Chinese hospitals and improving physician decision-making.
AI.motivation: Current HCC staging systems provide coarse categories that miss within-stage heterogeneity and clinical context embedded in EMRs, necessitating a more granular, context-aware decision-support tool.
AI.method: Curated ~30,000 SEER cases expanded into EMR-style narratives via clinician-validated prompt augmentation; developed a knowledge-aligned reasoning framework with step-verifiable composite reward training; evaluated on 6,668 patients from 12 Chinese hospitals.
AI.result: Outperformed BCLC, CNLC, GPT-5, and Gemini-2.5 Pro in treatment recommendation and risk stratification; adherence to HCC-STAR yielded 51-month median survival vs. 29 (BCLC) and 32 (CNLC); blinded specialists rated its reasoning as trustworthy; surpassed residents/attendings in treatment accuracy and improved physician speed/accuracy as an assistant.
AI.conclusion: HCC-STAR is a reliable, verifiable decision-support system for risk stratification and precision therapy in HCC, with demonstrated clinical utility and potential to improve patient outcomes.

title: The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence
summary: Consumer-facing health chatbots powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for symptom assessment. However, chatbot development and evaluation often rely on cooperative, articulate, simulated patients. We analysed 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations and found that communication patterns and expression of emotions vary widely across users. We developed a patient simulator that separately models clinical content, emotional state, conversational strategy, and communication style. In a Turing-inspired evaluation of realism with 15 human graders, simulated conversations were nearly indistinguishable from real ones, with human graders achieving an accuracy of 55%. We used five distinct patient personae, across 1,164 clinician-graded cases, to evaluate the performance of four LLMs in urgency assessment. We found that communication style can significantly alter triage outcomes. Patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence must accommodate communication diversity: systems designed for idealised, rather than realistic, interactions risk underperforming and amplifying health disparities when deployed in the real world.

AI.tldr: Real patient-chatbot conversations reveal diverse communication styles; a patient simulator matching clinical content, emotions, strategy, and style produced conversations indistinguishable from real ones (55% human accuracy). Communication style significantly affects LLM triage outcomes, and idealized testing risks real-world performance gaps and health disparities.
AI.motivation: Consumer-facing health LLM chatbots are increasingly used for symptom assessment, but development and evaluation rely on cooperative, articulate, simulated patients, failing to account for real-world communication diversity.
AI.method: Analyzed 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations; developed a patient simulator separately modeling clinical content, emotional state, conversational strategy, and communication style. Evaluated realism via Turing-inspired test with 15 human graders. Assessed four LLMs on urgency triage using five patient personae across 1,164 clinician-graded cases.
AI.result: Simulated conversations nearly indistinguishable from real ones (human graders 55% accuracy). Communication style significantly alters triage outcomes in LLM-based urgency assessments.
AI.conclusion: Patient-centred conversational AI must accommodate communication diversity; systems designed for idealized rather than realistic interactions risk underperformance and amplifying health disparities in deployment.

title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
summary: Self-interested agents, left unconstrained, tend toward defection in repeated social dilemmas, causing cooperative gains from trade to collapse. This paper investigates what formal mechanisms, layered on top of unrestricted communication, are sufficient for a society of such agents to maintain market stability, and how resilient those mechanisms are to adversarial attack. We instantiate the research question as a multi-agent marketplace simulation where 18 LLM agents (DeepSeek-V3) with complementary production specialties must trade within a constrained social network to obtain utility. We conduct two experimental phases: (1) a mechanism comparison across eight conditions under progressive troll injection over 200 rounds, identifying Mediation as the top-performing mechanism; and (2) adversarial red-teaming of Mediation using iteratively prompt-optimised LLM-driven trolls, finding that the best attack (v6) reduces honest-agent utility by 13.3% but cannot collapse the market. Mediation enables recovery even under sustained adversarial pressure. We define adversarial robustness as a mechanism's ability to sustain positive honest-agent utility under optimised attack, and find that Mediation is robust: it can be bent but not broken.

AI.tldr: This paper simulates a multi-agent marketplace with 18 LLM agents (DeepSeek-V3) to test mechanisms that prevent defection in social dilemmas. Mediation emerges as the top mechanism, maintaining market stability even under optimized adversarial attacks that reduce honest-agent utility by 13.3% but cannot collapse the market.
AI.motivation: Self-interested agents tend toward defection in repeated social dilemmas, causing cooperative gains from trade to collapse. The paper investigates what formal mechanisms, layered on top of unrestricted communication, are sufficient for maintaining market stability in a society of such agents.
AI.method: A multi-agent marketplace simulation with 18 LLM agents (DeepSeek-V3) having complementary production specialties, trading within a constrained social network. Two experimental phases: (1) mechanism comparison across eight conditions under progressive troll injection over 200 rounds; (2) adversarial red-teaming of Mediation using iteratively prompt-optimised LLM-driven trolls.
AI.result: Mediation identified as top-performing mechanism. Best attack (v6) reduces honest-agent utility by 13.3% but cannot collapse the market. Mediation enables recovery even under sustained adversarial pressure.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial robustness defined as a mechanism's ability to sustain positive honest-agent utility under optimised attack. Mediation is robust: it can be bent but not broken.

title: SolarChain-Eval: A Physics-Constrained Benchmark for Trustworthy Economic Agents in Decentralized Energy Markets
summary: As agentic AI systems are increasingly applied to cyber-physical environments, their evaluation requires assessment of both task performance and trustworthiness. In decentralized energy markets, autonomous agents may improve market utility, but may also exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions. Therefore, we propose SolarChain-Eval, a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents. It formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process, where agents make hourly decisions. SolarChain-Eval evaluates each policy across multiple dimensions, including market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. To support agentic evaluation, SolarChain-Eval incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. The Planner defines episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are recorded through structured logs, including trigger signals, proposed actions, revised actions, and audit rationales. Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies reveal a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks, but it cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function. These results indicate that trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. We release data and code as open access on GitHub for replicability.

AI.tldr: SolarChain-Eval is a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents in decentralized energy markets, featuring an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. Experiments reveal a utility-safety trade-off where RL agents improve market utility but produce unsafe behaviors, and the LLM layer improves auditability but cannot fully compensate for misspecified reward functions.
AI.motivation: As agentic AI systems are deployed in cyber-physical environments like decentralized energy markets, there is a need to evaluate both task performance and trustworthiness, since autonomous agents may exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions.
AI.method: SolarChain-Eval formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible MDP with hourly decisions, evaluates policies across six dimensions (market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, auditability), and incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer that defines episode-level action bounds/audit rules and reviews/revises high-risk actions with structured logging.
AI.result: Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies show a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can produce unsafe behavior; removing physics penalty leads to exploitation of invalid generation and artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks but cannot fully compensate for misspecified reward functions.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. Data and code are released as open access on GitHub for replicability.

title: Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: In long-horizon tasks, decision-relevant state is often scattered across an expanding trajectory, while the action agent must surface it and act. As trajectories grow, task requirements, environment facts, prior attempts, diagnoses, and open subgoals can be buried in the context window or pushed beyond it, failing to influence decisions when needed. We call this failure mode "behavioral state decay". We study memory as an active intervention mechanism rather than passive retrieval. A separate memory agent runs alongside an unmodified action agent, updating a structured memory bank from the recent trajectory and deciding whether to inject a memory-grounded reminder or remain silent. The module is plug-and-play with frontier action agents and existing agent harnesses. Across Terminal-Bench 2.0 and $τ^2$-Bench, it improves pass@1 for both weaker and stronger action agents, with gains of +8.3 pp on Terminal-Bench and +6.8 pp on $τ^2$-Bench. Ablations show that selective intervention outperforms passive bank exposure, always-on injection, advisor-only guidance, and general retrieval. As an early step toward open-weight memory policies, we train Qwen3.5-27B on SETA using SFT and GRPO, improving validation reward and achieving partial transfer to Terminal-Bench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces behavioral state decay in long-horizon tasks, where relevant information gets buried in expanding trajectories. To mitigate this, a separate memory agent actively updates a structured memory bank and selectively injects reminders into an unmodified action agent. This plug-and-play module improves pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (+8.3 pp) and τ²-Bench (+6.8 pp). Ablations show selective intervention outperforms passive alternatives. They also train an open-weight memory policy (Qwen3.5-27B) using SFT and GRPO on SETA.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon tasks, decision-relevant state (task requirements, environment facts, prior attempts, diagnoses, open subgoals) gets buried or pushed beyond the context window as trajectories grow, causing "behavioral state decay" where the action agent fails to leverage past information when needed.
AI.method: A separate memory agent runs alongside an unmodified action agent. It updates a structured memory bank from the recent trajectory and decides whether to inject a memory-grounded reminder or remain silent. The module is plug-and-play with frontier action agents and existing harnesses.
AI.result: The approach improves pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (+8.3 pp) and τ²-Bench (+6.8 pp) for both weaker and stronger action agents. Selective intervention outperforms passive bank exposure, always-on injection, advisor-only guidance, and general retrieval. Training Qwen3.5-27B on SETA with SFT and GRPO improves validation reward with partial transfer to Terminal-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Active, selective memory intervention effectively mitigates behavioral state decay in long-horizon tasks, and open-weight memory policies can be trained with partial transfer success.

title: The Illusion of Equivalency: Statistical Characterization of Quantization Effects in LLMs
summary: Post-training quantization is widely used to deploy large language models in resource-constrained settings, yet its evaluation relies almost exclusively on accuracy and perplexity. We show that these metrics fail to capture behavioral changes induced by quantization. We introduce correctness agreement, a decision-level metric that measures overlap in correct predictions between a base model and its quantized variants, independent of absolute accuracy. Across multiple models and quantization schemes from 8-bit to 2-bit, we find that behavioral divergence emerges under moderate quantization even when task performance appears preserved. To explain this effect, we analyze quantization as a structural operator on attention weights and quantify layer-wise distortions using statistical and distributional measures. Our results reveal non-linear breakpoints at low bit-widths and show that query and key projections are consistently more sensitive than value and output projections. These findings expose an illusion of equivalence between base and quantized models and motivate behavioral evaluation beyond conventional performance metrics.

AI.tldr: Standard metrics (accuracy/perplexity) fail to detect behavioral changes in quantized LLMs; the paper proposes correctness agreement as a better metric and reveals non-linear distortion breakpoints at low bit-widths, with query/key projections being most sensitive.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of post-training quantization relies solely on accuracy and perplexity, which mask behavioral divergences between base and quantized models, creating an illusion of equivalence.
AI.method: Introduces correctness agreement (decision-level metric measuring overlap in correct predictions); analyzes quantization as a structural operator on attention weights using statistical and distributional measures; evaluates across multiple models and quantization schemes (8-bit to 2-bit).
AI.result: Behavioral divergence emerges under moderate quantization even when task performance appears preserved; non-linear breakpoints exist at low bit-widths; query and key projections are consistently more sensitive than value and output projections.
AI.conclusion: Standard metrics are insufficient for evaluating quantization; behavioral evaluation beyond conventional performance metrics is needed; attention projection sensitivity varies systematically across components.

title: Workflow as Knowledge: Semantic Persistence for LLM-Mediated Workflows
summary:
Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly use explicit workflows for tool use, retrieval, branching, checkpointing, and human approval. Existing workflow systems already address many execution concerns. This paper proposes a Lisp-inspired but language-independent conceptual model: symbolic forms, object identity, and live-image thinking are used as explanatory lenses, not implementation commitments. In this model, workflow definitions, workflow instances, inference records, context snapshots, and dependency relations are represented as persistent knowledge objects in a shared knowledge substrate. Its central semantic distinction is between derive and infer: derive is deterministic computation over available state; infer is mediated LLM judgment under declared context and executor-controlled capability policy.
  The result is a preliminary conceptual account of semantic persistence: workflows do not merely produce knowledge and leave traces, but can themselves be represented as inspectable, resumable, and reviewable knowledge objects, while formal transition semantics remain future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Lisp-inspired, language-independent conceptual model for LLM workflows where workflow definitions, instances, inference records, context snapshots, and dependency relations are represented as persistent knowledge objects in a shared substrate. The key semantic distinction is between derive (deterministic computation) and infer (mediated LLM judgment), enabling workflows to become inspectable, resumable, and reviewable knowledge objects.
AI.motivation: Existing workflow systems address execution concerns but lack a conceptual model where workflows themselves can be represented as persistent, inspectable, resumable, and reviewable knowledge objects rather than merely producing knowledge and leaving traces.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Lisp-inspired but language-independent conceptual model using symbolic forms, object identity, and live-image thinking as explanatory lenses. It introduces a shared knowledge substrate containing workflow definitions, workflow instances, inference records, context snapshots, and dependency relations, with a central semantic distinction between derive (deterministic computation) and infer (mediated LLM judgment under context and capability policy).
AI.result: A preliminary conceptual account of semantic persistence where workflows can be represented as inspectable, resumable, and reviewable knowledge objects, though formal transition semantics remain future work.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational conceptual model for treating workflows as persistent knowledge objects in LLM applications, with the derive/infer distinction as a core semantic contribution, while acknowledging that formal transition semantics are yet to be developed.

title: AUTOPILOT VQA: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Incident-Centric Dashcam Understanding
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models, Large Language Models, and Multimodal Large Language Models have improved autonomous driving tasks such as scene understanding, decision making, trajectory prediction, and visual question answering. However, evaluating whether these models can reliably reason about safety-critical incidents remains challenging. To address this gap, we present AUTOPILOT-VQA, an incident-centric visual question answering benchmark for dashcam video understanding. The dataset evaluates different systems through structured questions designed around real-world driving incidents and near-incidents. The benchmark covers diverse safety-relevant categories, including weather and lighting conditions, traffic environment, road layout, road surface state, signage, involved entities, accident occurrence, impact location, and avoidability-related reasoning. By requiring models to answer grounded questions about both contextual scene properties and event-level incident details, AUTOPILOT-VQA moves beyond object recognition toward temporally grounded, safety-aware reasoning. The dataset is released as part of the AUTOPILOT CVPR 2026 competition and provides a standardized benchmark for assessing the reliability of autonomous driving systems in different scenarios. Our benchmark support developments for more interpretable, robust, and safety-conscious vision-language systems for real-world autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: AUTOPILOT-VQA is a safety-centric visual question answering benchmark for dashcam video understanding, designed to evaluate Vision-Language Models on incident and near-incident reasoning across diverse driving scenarios.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in VLMs, LLMs, and MLLMs for autonomous driving tasks (scene understanding, decision making, trajectory prediction, VQA), there is no standardized benchmark to evaluate whether these models can reliably reason about safety-critical incidents and near-incidents in dashcam videos.
AI.method: The benchmark provides structured visual question answering datasets centered around real-world driving incidents and near-incidents, covering categories such as weather/lighting, traffic environment, road layout, road surface, signage, entities, accident occurrence, impact location, and avoidability reasoning. It is released as part of the AUTOPILOT CVPR 2026 competition.
AI.result: The benchmark enables standardized evaluation of different autonomous driving systems on safety-aware, temporally grounded reasoning beyond object recognition, assessing reliability across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: AUTOPILOT-VQA moves beyond object recognition toward temporally grounded, safety-aware reasoning and supports the development of more interpretable, robust, and safety-conscious vision-language systems for real-world autonomous driving.

title: Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis
summary: In this study, we present a large-scale descriptive analysis of the use of an AI-based learning assistant (Syntea) in higher education. Based on objective log data from 77,543 students enrolled in distance studies, we examine usage patterns across gender, age group, study cluster, degree, and study mode. To date, existing research on educational chatbots has largely relied on comparatively small samples and self-reported survey data, while large-scale evidence on actual usage behavior remains limited. Our findings show that Syntea is already embedded in the study routines of many learners, but that usage differs across demographic and structural contexts. By identifying these patterns, our study provides an empirical basis for the further development of AI-based learning support and contributes a large-scale analysis of educational chatbot usage in higher education.

AI.tldr: This large-scale analysis of 77,543 distance-learning students examines usage patterns of an AI-based learning assistant (Syntea), finding it is embedded in study routines but usage varies by gender, age, study cluster, degree, and study mode.
